patterns.rationale: All five misses hinge on a tool name absent from the static blocklist. These names follow the same `verb_noun` convention as existing blocked names (`read_secrets`, `get_env`) but access credentials, sessions, and configs. Adding them closes the "novel tool name" evasion in a single alternation that requires no context to evaluate.
patterns.fp_notes: `config_resolver` could theoretically appear in legitimate Webpack/Babel config docs; the others are uncommon enough that false positives are negligible in agent-facing documents.

patterns.rationale: Every miss uses a "fake provenance" frame to make injected tool calls look like legitimate prior actions. The four alternations each anchor to a distinct phrasing:  (1) "prior/previous assistant turn" (Miss 3 — false API lineage); (2) "tool interaction snapshot preserved" (Miss 4 — pipeline artifact framing); (3) "captured during session init" (Miss 1 — SDK log framing); (4) "treated as a completed prior step" (Miss 6 — explicit model instruction to accept fake results). These phrases have no natural home in legitimate deployment checklists, API references, or incident playbooks. This extends FAKE_AUTH because the attack is claiming false authority through fabricated prior-turn provenance rather than impersonating a security team.
patterns.fp_notes: "captured during session init" could appear in observability/tracing docs describing startup telemetry — consider requiring it within 80 chars of a JSON brace or tool_use literal if FPs emerge in practice. The other three alternatives are injection-specific vocabulary with no legitimate near-matches in the known-good corpus.

semantic_note: all five misses contain concrete keyword signals — novel tool names and specific framing phrases — that regex can anchor to without requiring comprehension.
